sections.overview: The black rat, also called the roof or ship rat, is a small, adaptable rodent whose fortunes have travelled with people. The IUCN assessment describes its original range as Indomalayan; maritime trade carried it far beyond that region, and established populations now occur on many continents and islands. It thrives in settlements as well as forests, so “house rat” describes an association, not a habitat limit.
sections.identification: A black rat is usually slender, with a pointed muzzle, prominent thin ears and a tail longer than its head and body together. Coat colour is variable: animals may be blackish, charcoal, brown or lighter above, often paler below. The brown rat (Rattus norvegicus) is generally heavier and stockier, with a shorter, thicker tail and a blunter muzzle. Colour alone is unreliable, and young rats can be hard to identify. Adults have a head-and-body length of about 16.5–20.5 cm, a tail of 18.5–25.5 cm and a reported mass of 95–340 g; these ranges are not separated by sex.
sections.habitat: This species uses warm coastal districts, farms, gardens, woodland and buildings, especially where food and shelter occur together. Its climbing ability makes shrubs, tree crowns, vines, fences, wires and roof spaces accessible; nests can be built above ground in vegetation or structures. In California, roof rats often nest in trees and dense landscaping, but also descend to the ground to forage or feed within trees. They may burrow or use ground-level shelter when elevated sites are scarce, so arboreality is a tendency rather than a rule.
sections.diet: Black rats eat a broad range of foods, usually with a strong plant component: fruit, berries, seeds, nuts, grain, leaves and other vegetation. They also take invertebrates and, where available, eggs or small animals. In four Galápagos petrel colonies sampled on San Cristóbal in June 2013, stomach contents were mostly plant material and arthropods; seeds of the native tree Miconia robinsoniana were especially common. That snapshot is local and seasonal, not a universal menu. The species can shift toward foods that are abundant at a particular site.
sections.behavior: Black rats are mainly active at night, when darkness helps them forage while reducing exposure to many daytime predators. They are not invariably solitary: species accounts report groups containing several males and females, with dominance affecting access to mates and defended food territories. The available descriptions do not establish one social structure for every population. Calls, scent deposits and postures provide cues during social contact. Daily routes link nests to food patches, running along branches, fences and overhead lines as well as across the ground.
sections.reproduction: Where food and shelter remain available, black rats can breed repeatedly; gestation is short, about three to four weeks, and a litter commonly contains several young. Newborns are helpless, naked and blind. The mother nurses and protects them in a nest; fur and mobility develop during the first weeks, and weaning follows after roughly three to four weeks. Young may become reproductively mature within a few months, allowing numbers to rebound quickly. Yet reproduction is not equally continuous everywhere: a 2024 study across Madagascar found strong seasonal variation inside and outside homes, associated partly with rainfall, habitat and rat density.
sections.ecology: The rat’s climbing and omnivory connect it to food webs both above and below ground. It may disperse some seeds after eating fruit, but it also consumes seeds and can damage seedlings; whether its net effect benefits a plant depends on the species and setting. In Sydney’s urban bushland remnants, a field experiment found that black rats attacked bird nests, adding a source of nest mortality where they had replaced native bush rats. Their greater use of trees, aided by a longer tail that improves balance, can expose arboreal nests and other tree-dwelling animals to predation.
sections.conservation: The amended IUCN global assessment, published in 2021 from an assessment dated 7 September 2016, lists the species as Least Concern because it is widespread and abundant. This global category does not mean harmless: introductions can severely affect local wildlife. On Lord Howe Island, Australia, the black rat arrived after a shipwreck in 1918; a 2000 state scientific determination linked it to losses of endemic birds and the disappearance of the Lord Howe Island stick insect from the main island, threats to native land snails, and reduced palm seed yields. Management concerns are therefore local ecosystem impacts, not global extinction risk. The Island Board’s November 2025 final report confirmed successful rodent eradication and emphasized continued biosecurity to prevent reintroduction.
